title: Interface-engineered oxidation-resistant wafer-level Tantalum-Tantalum thermocompression bonding for 3D integration of superconducting interconnects
authors: Harsh Mishra, Ullas Pandey, Sathish Bonam, Adirae Dinesh, Sai Rama Krishna Malladi, Shiv Govind Singh
abstract: Wafer-level 3D integration of superconducting interconnects requires low-thermal budget bonding processes compatible with superconducting materials. Rapid native oxide formation on tantalum (Ta) surfaces limits low-temperature, low-pressure direct Ta-Ta thermocompression bonding. In this study, we develop an oxidation-resistant bonding process using an ultrathin Au passivation layer to suppress oxide formation during bonding. The engineered interface enables blanket Ta-Ta wafer bonding at 300 $^\circ$C under 4.93 bar, significantly reducing the bonding thermal budget and generation of $α$-Ta across the interface, which potentially improves coherence time as reported in literature. Structural and interfacial analyses confirm oxide suppression and continuous metallic bonding, having a bond strength of 169 MPa. This work demonstrates a low-temperature, low-pressure Ta-Ta thermocompression bonding strategy for scalable 3D superconducting interconnect integration.
summary: This research addresses the challenge of bonding Tantalum superconducting interconnects for 3D integration by using an ultrathin Gold passivation layer. This technique suppresses detrimental oxide formation, allowing a strong, reliable bond to be formed at a significantly lower temperature ($300^\circ	ext{C}$). The results demonstrate a robust method enabling scalable fabrication for advanced electronic and quantum devices.
main_problem: The primary challenge is achieving low-thermal budget, low-pressure direct Tantalum (Ta)–Tantalum thermocompression bonding necessary for 3D integration of superconducting interconnects.
main_result: Applying an ultrathin Au passivation layer successfully enables strong Ta–Ta bonding at a reduced temperature ($300^\circ	ext{C}$) while maintaining high bond strength ($\sim 169 	ext{ MPa}$), which is crucial for superconducting applications.
method: The study employed surface analysis (AFM, XPS), mechanical testing (shear tests), and structural characterization (FESEM/TEM) to validate the bonding process using Au as a protective barrier layer.
model_or_system: The physical system is wafer-level 3D integration utilizing superconducting interconnects made of Tantalum (Ta). The methodology involves depositing an ultrathin Gold (Au) passivation layer onto Ta surfaces before performing thermocompression bonding.
key_observables: Bond strength ($\sim 169 	ext{ MPa}$), surface roughness ($R_q = 0.177 	ext{ nm}$), and retention of superconducting critical temperature ($T_c$).
important_parameters: Bonding Temperature ($300^\circ	ext{C}$ vs $500^\circ	ext{C}$), Au passivation thickness (optimal at 3 nm), and bonding pressure (4.93 bar).
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the Au layer effectively suppresses rapid native oxide formation on Ta, thereby allowing low-temperature bonding compatible with superconducting materials.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the schematic of Au passivation suppressing oxidation and the setup/results of tensile shear tests demonstrating high bond strength retention even after a 7-day pause.
paper_structure: The paper follows a structure detailing the scientific problem, proposing the Au passivation solution, characterizing the process using multiple analytical techniques (AFM, XPS, mechanical testing), presenting results showing improved bonding metrics compared to unpassivated samples, and concluding with its viability for scalable 3D integration.
why_interesting: While not directly related to quantum information theory itself, this work is highly relevant to superconducting circuit fabrication, which forms the physical backbone of many quantum computing architectures (e.g., Josephson junctions). The focus on low-loss, high-reliability interconnects is critical for scaling up any solid-state quantum device.
